claims.text: Enhancing atomic-scale surface homogeneity in nanoscale PtPdRhRuIrOs catalysts will improve durability during ethanol oxidation.
The durability improvement will result from reduced localized oxidation of vulnerable components.
The as-synthesized PtPdRhRuIrOs catalyst has a moderately homogeneous but nonoptimized surface atomic distribution.
Controlled thermal annealing will enhance atomic intermixing in the PtPdRhRuIrOs nanoparticles.
Controlled thermal annealing will reduce minor elemental segregation at the nanoparticle surfaces.
Alkaline electrolyte at approximately 60–80°C represents typical moderate conditions for ethanol oxidation in this system.
Several hours of operation will be sufficient to reveal durability trends.
A more uniform surface distribution of the constituent elements will improve inter-element electronic interactions.
Localized oxide phases can initiate catalyst deactivation during ethanol oxidation.
A more even electronic environment will reduce the susceptibility of specific surface sites to aggressive oxidation.
The annealed catalyst will maintain a more stable catalytic current than the as-synthesized catalyst during prolonged ethanol oxidation.
The annealed catalyst will undergo less change in surface oxidation state than the as-synthesized catalyst.
Greater current stability is indicative of sustained catalytic activity.
The proposed homogeneity-mediated mechanism should hold under moderately alkaline ethanol oxidation at approximately 60–80°C.
Extreme pH, extreme temperatures, or strong corrosives could independently drive oxidation and invalidate the proposed mechanism.
Thermal annealing may cause particle coarsening or changes in particle-size distribution.
Annealing-induced particle coarsening or size-distribution changes may independently influence catalytic performance.
